greek_apollod_heracles.name: Slay beasts with bare hands and overwhelming might
greek_apollod_heracles.notes: Strangled the invulnerable Nemean lion whose hide no weapon could pierce, then skinned it with its own claws (First Labour).

greek_apollod_heracles.name: Ascend from the funeral pyre to immortality and Olympus
greek_apollod_heracles.notes: After self-immolation on Mt. Oeta, his mortal part was burned away and he was taken up to heaven, reconciled with Hera and wedded to Hebe.

greek_apollod_perseus.name: Behead the Gorgon Medusa while she sleeps
greek_apollod_perseus.notes: Approached the only mortal Gorgon, viewing her reflection in his bronze shield to avoid her petrifying gaze, and struck off her head with the harpe.

greek_apollod_perseus.name: Slay the sea-monster Cetus to free Andromeda
greek_apollod_perseus.notes: Swooping from the air in winged sandals, he killed the sea-beast sent against Andromeda and won her as his bride.

greek_apollod_andromeda.name: Offered as expiatory sacrifice to the sea-monster
greek_apollod_andromeda.notes: Chained to a sea-cliff as a sacrifice to Cetus to atone for her mother Cassiopeia's boast against the Nereids; rescued and wed by Perseus.

greek_apollod_danae.name: Conceive Perseus from Zeus's golden rain
greek_apollod_danae.notes: Imprisoned in a bronze chamber, she was reached by Zeus in the form of a shower of gold and bore Perseus.

greek_apollod_megara.name: First wife of Heracles, bearer of his Theban children
greek_apollod_megara.notes: Given to Heracles by her father Creon for delivering Thebes from the Minyans; she and her children were slain by Heracles in his Hera-sent madness.

greek_apollod_niobe.name: Boast of fertility against the goddess Leto
greek_apollod_niobe.notes: Vaunted her twelve (or fourteen) children as superior to Leto's two, provoking Apollo and Artemis to slay them.

greek_apollod_niobe.name: Petrify into an ever-weeping stone
greek_apollod_niobe.notes: Transformed on Mt. Sipylus into a rock that perpetually sheds tears for her dead children.

greek_apollod_omphale.name: Purchase and command the enslaved Heracles
greek_apollod_omphale.notes: The Lydian queen bought Heracles as a slave for the term of servitude imposed by the oracle for the killing of Iphitus, setting him to women's labours.

greek_apollod_auge.name: Serve as virgin priestess of Athena Alea
greek_apollod_auge.notes: Made priestess of Athena at Tegea under vow of chastity by her father Aleus; violated by Heracles and bore Telephus.

greek_apollod_acrisius.name: Imprison Danae to thwart the oracle of his death
greek_apollod_acrisius.notes: Warned that his daughter's son would kill him, he shut Danae in a bronze underground chamber; the prophecy was fulfilled when Perseus's discus struck him.

greek_apollod_amphitryon.name: Lead the war against the Teleboans and Taphians
greek_apollod_amphitryon.notes: As exiled Mycenaean prince he commanded the campaign avenging Electryon's sons, victory over Pterelaus' people preceding the night of Heracles' conception.

greek_apollod_electryon.name: Rule Mycenae and wage the Taphian cattle-war
greek_apollod_electryon.notes: Succeeded to the Mycenaean kingship after Perseus and fought the Taphians and Teleboans over the rustling of his cattle and the death of his sons.

greek_apollod_hyllus.name: Lead the first Heraclid return to the Peloponnese
greek_apollod_hyllus.notes: Eldest son of Heracles and Deianira; led the Heraclidae homeward and fell in single combat against Echemus of Tegea at the Isthmus.

greek_apollod_iphicles.name: Mortal twin-brother and war-companion of Heracles
greek_apollod_iphicles.notes: Son of Amphitryon born the same night as Heracles; fought beside him and was father of Iolaus.

greek_antiope_thebes.name: Bear the divine twins Amphion and Zethus to Zeus
greek_antiope_thebes.notes: Visited by Zeus in the guise of a satyr; bore the twin founders of Thebes, who avenged her persecution by Dirce.

greek_apollod_iole.name: Be the prize and unwitting cause of Heracles' death
greek_apollod_iole.notes: Won by Heracles at the sack of Oechalia; jealousy over her drove Deianira to send the poisoned robe; by Heracles' dying command she was wed to Hyllus.

greek_apollod_cresphontes.name: Rule Messenia as Heraclid king
greek_apollod_cresphontes.notes: Won the richest portion, Messenia, in the division of the Peloponnese among the Heraclidae and founded its royal house before his murder by Polyphontes.

greek_apollod_aristodemus.name: Progenitor of the dual Spartan kingship
greek_apollod_aristodemus.notes: Heraclid to whom Laconia fell; father of the twins Eurysthenes and Procles from whom the two Spartan royal houses descend.

greek_apollod_argeia.name: Mother of the Spartan twin-kings
greek_apollod_argeia.notes: Bore Eurysthenes and Procles and refused to name the elder, founding the Spartan dual-kingship dispute.

greek_apollod_machaon.name: Heal battle-wounds by the surgeon's art
greek_apollod_machaon.notes: The Achaean army-physician who extracted the arrow and treated Menelaus' wound at Troy; later himself wounded and tended.

greek_apollod_acamas.name: Serve as Achaean envoy demanding Helen's return
greek_apollod_acamas.notes: With Diomedes (in some accounts) went to Troy before the war to demand restitution of Helen; later among the warriors in the Wooden Horse.

greek_apollod_hippolytus.name: Hunting gear of the chaste huntsman

greek_apollod_heracles.name: Heracleia
greek_apollod_heracles.notes: Festivals at the Cynosarges gymnasium and at Marathon in Attica; Heracles received a twofold cult, sacrificed to first as a chthonic hero with a libation and then as an Olympian god upon an altar (Pindar's heros theos).

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 2.44; Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.15.3; 1.19.3

greek_apollod_perseus.name: Hero-cult of Perseus
greek_apollod_perseus.notes: Worshipped as a hero at Mycenae (shrine on the Mycenae-Argos road and the spring Persea), and chiefly, in Pausanias' day, at Seriphos and Athens.

greek_apollod_iolaus.name: Iolaeia
greek_apollod_iolaus.notes: Athletic and equestrian games at Thebes at the heroon of Iolaus by the Proetidian gate; lovers exchanged vows of fidelity at his tomb. Also worshipped with Heracles in Sardinia (the Iolaeis).

sources.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.23.1; Pindar, Olympian 9.98-99

greek_apollod_hippolytus.name: Cult of Hippolytus at Troezen
greek_apollod_hippolytus.notes: Maidens of Troezen dedicated a lock of hair to Hippolytus before marriage at his precinct and temple; he was honoured with annual lamentations.

sources.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece 2.32.1; Euripides, Hippolytus 1423-1430

greek_apollod_machaon.name: Healing hero-shrine of Machaon at Gerenia
greek_apollod_machaon.notes: Tomb and sanctuary at Gerenia in Messenia where the sick sought cures; a bronze statue stood crowned at the holy place called Rhodos.

greek_apollod_gorgasus.name: Healing sanctuary of Gorgasus and Nicomachus at Pharae
greek_apollod_gorgasus.notes: Shrine at Pharae in Messenia, built by Isthmius son of Glaucus, where sacrifices and votive offerings were brought for the cure of disease and injury.

greek_apollod_nicomachus.name: Healing sanctuary of Gorgasus and Nicomachus at Pharae
greek_apollod_nicomachus.notes: Shared sanctuary at Pharae in Messenia receiving sacrifices and votives for healing, the inherited power of the Asclepiad line.

greek_apollod_eurystheus.name: Protective tomb-cult in Attica
greek_apollod_eurystheus.notes: Executed near Athens, his buried body was made a protective talisman against future invading Heraclidae; his head was buried apart at Tricorythus by the spring Macaria and his body before the temple of Athena at Pallene.

greek_apollod_podalirius.name: Incubation oracle of Podalirius in Daunia
greek_apollod_podalirius.notes: In Daunian Italy a hero-oracle of Podalirius where suppliants slept on sheepskins to receive healing dreams by his tomb on Mt. Drion.

attributes.name: Lion-skin cloak and knotted club
attributes.notes: Canonically shown wrapped in the Nemean lion's pelt (head as a helm) and wielding a heavy club of wild-olive wood, often bearded as an older hero.

sources.reference: Pausanias, Description of Greece 5.25.7 (bronze of Heracles with club and bow)

attributes.name: Bow and quiver
attributes.notes: Frequently carries the bow with which he shot the Stymphalian birds and the centaur Nessus, the arrows envenomed with Hydra's gall.

sacredPlants.name: White poplar (leuke)
sacredPlants.notes: At Olympia Heracles burned the victims' thighs on white-poplar wood brought from the Acheron; the leaf became his emblematic plant.

sacredPlants.name: Wild olive (kotinos)
sacredPlants.notes: Said to have brought the wild olive to Olympia from the land of the Hyperboreans, its branches becoming the victor's crown.

attributes.name: Winged sandals and curved sword
attributes.notes: Depicted as a youthful hero in winged sandals and the cap of invisibility, brandishing the harpe and bearing Medusa's severed head in a wallet.

attributes.name: The Gorgon's head (gorgoneion)
attributes.notes: Carries Medusa's head, whose gaze turns onlookers to stone, in the kibisis until he gives it to Athena.

attributes.name: Veiled mother shielding a dying child
attributes.notes: Rendered in the Niobid group as a mantled woman drawing her robe over a child as the divine arrows fall; her petrified form on Sipylus seems to weep when seen from afar.

attributes.name: Chaste huntsman with horses and chariot
attributes.notes: Shown as a youthful hunter devoted to Artemis, associated with horses and the runaway chariot by which Poseidon's bull destroyed him.

sacredPlants.name: Flowers of the untrodden meadow
sacredPlants.notes: Wove for Artemis a garland from an inviolate meadow where no flock grazes, emblem of his purity.

attributes.name: Lion-skin and club borne by the queen
attributes.notes: Iconography of role-reversal: Omphale shoulders Heracles' lion-skin and grasps his club while the hero, in female dress, spins wool at the distaff.

attributes.name: Maiden chained to the sea-rock
attributes.notes: The canonical image: Andromeda bound to a coastal crag awaiting the monster, often shown at the moment of Perseus' rescue.
